title: Embedded Linux Platform Engineering

standard.family: AutoLeaP Embedded Systems Body of Knowledge

summary: Embedded Linux is a product platform, not only a kernel. The bootloader, kernel, Device Tree, firmware, root filesystem, init system, services, package composition and update mechanism form one validated release. Kernel boot completion does not equal product readiness; the architecture must define when required devices, services and customer functions are available.
learningObjectives: Trace Linux boot, device binding and service readiness.
Explain kernel/user-space boundaries and Device Tree responsibilities.
Plan a maintainable long-life Linux distribution and update model.
explanation: Embedded Linux is a product platform, not only a kernel. The bootloader, kernel, Device Tree, firmware, root filesystem, init system, services, package composition and update mechanism form one validated release. Kernel boot completion does not equal product readiness; the architecture must define when required devices, services and customer functions are available.

The Linux device model binds device instances to drivers through bus-specific matching. Device Tree describes non-discoverable hardware and resources such as interrupts, clocks, regulators and memory. Drivers should use kernel frameworks rather than hard-coded board knowledge. Probe deferral is a dependency mechanism, but persistent deferral usually reveals missing or circular platform dependencies.

Long-lived products need a kernel and distribution support strategy. Downstream patches, vendor BSP dependencies, CVE intake, reproducible builds, module compatibility and hardware regression require explicit ownership. Yocto or Buildroot assembles the product, but metadata discipline and continuous integration determine whether the system remains reproducible.
whyItMatters: Linux defects often emerge at the boundary between hardware, kernel, services and product configuration.
A controlled platform lifecycle is essential when field support lasts longer than the original development program.
activities: Define boot and service dependency graph
Design Device Tree and driver ownership
Instrument scheduler, memory, I/O and boot performance
outputs: Linux platform composition and support policy
automotiveExample: A telematics gateway uses an LTS kernel with a small tracked vendor patch set, a read-only A/B root filesystem, and a separate schema-controlled data partition. Device Tree schemas validate board variants. Product readiness is declared only when modem, secure storage and vehicle-network services pass health checks.
commonMistakes: Treating Device Tree as arbitrary product configuration
Accepting an unsupported vendor kernel without lifecycle cost
Using aggregate CPU statistics to diagnose latency
Loading all drivers as modules without boot dependency analysis
Allowing writable system files to defeat reproducible updates
